title: The death in the bath
hookLine: Tacitus tells of Seneca's slow death and Paulina's survival (Annals 15.63–64)

cards: We told the outline of this story back in year one: Nero's order, the friends at the table, the image of a life.
Today we go back to Tacitus and read it more slowly, because the part people usually skip is who was in the room. It's the year 65, at a country house four miles outside Rome.
Seneca is at dinner with his wife, Paulina, and two friends, when the soldiers arrive.

teach.h: PAULINA: I WILL DIE WITH YOU.
teach.b: First, Paulina. When the order comes, Tacitus says, Paulina declares that she will die with him. Seneca had spent years writing about not clinging to life, and he doesn't forbid her.
He tells her he had shown her ways to go on living, but if she chooses this, he won't stand in the way of her courage. Second, the other room. Then Seneca does something quietly tender.
He asks that she be taken to another room, so that neither of them, watching the other suffer, would lose heart. Even at the end, he's thinking about what being beside someone does to them.
Third, the slow hours. Seneca's body was old and thin from plain living, Tacitus says, and his life left it slowly. Through those hours he kept the people around him busy and steady.
He called for his secretaries and dictated, and Tacitus doesn't repeat it, because it had already been published. At the last he was carried into a warm bath, and there he died.
Fourth, Paulina lives. Nero, not wanting a reputation for extra cruelty, ordered her saved, and her household bound her wounds. Here Tacitus is careful.
Some at the time claimed she had sought death only while she believed Nero couldn't be softened.

He reports the gossip, then what he knows: she lived a few more years, faithful to her husband's memory, so pale it was plain how much life had drained from her. Tacitus doesn't make her a statue. He lets her be a person.
And he leaves a picture worth keeping: a death surrounded, start to finish, by people who stayed beside him.

how: Readers of Tacitus's account of Seneca's death often notice less the death itself than the people around him, and take from it a reminder to stay near those who are suffering.

practice: This is a heavy story, so go gently.

Think of someone you'd want beside you on a hard day, not the hardest, just a hard one, and picture their face and voice; then turn it around, and hold for a few breaths someone whose hard day you could sit beside.
